text: Everything so far in this chapter has been about writing access correctly in the first place — scoped policies, organization-wide guardrails, roles over long-lived keys. This lesson covers the tool that catches what gets through anyway: IAM Access Analyzer, built to answer one specific question for every resource that supports a resource-based policy.

That question is whether anything outside your zone of trust can reach a given resource. A zone of trust is either a single account or an entire Organization, and you choose which when you create the analyzer. Everything inside it is trusted by default. Access Analyzer checks this by mathematically evaluating the actual policy logic, not pattern-matching keywords, across S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, Lambda functions, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets, and more.

A real finding tells you exactly what you need to decide. This one says the ltv-shared-reports bucket is reachable by an external role in a different account, with GetObject and ListBucket permissions and no condition narrowing it. Sometimes that's genuinely intentional — a vendor needing read access — and you archive it with a rule so the same known pattern doesn't resurface as noise. Other times it's a bucket policy copied from another project with a wildcard principal nobody meant to leave in.

A newer finding type looks the other direction, flagging access that exists but isn't actually used: IAM roles that haven't been assumed recently, access keys with no recent API calls, passwords that haven't signed in, and unused permissions — individual actions a policy grants that the principal has simply never called. That last one targets the real gap between least privilege as written and least privilege as actually exercised.

Access Analyzer doesn't only scan what's deployed — it checks policies while you're writing them. Policy validation runs over a hundred checks for syntax errors and overly permissive patterns. check-no-new-access compares a proposed change against a reference policy and flags anything newly granted. check-access-not-granted lets you assert that specific actions should never be reachable at all, which fits directly into a CI/CD pipeline as a gate before a policy change merges.

That closes out AWS identity security for this chapter: scoped policies, organization-wide SCP guardrails, roles over long-lived keys, and Access Analyzer catching what still gets through. Next chapter moves to the network layer, comparing NSGs and security groups across both clouds.
